edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id after a slash, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / K1-1", on every page (template change).

edits.quote: It is your turn with a bigger pile. Circle the counters you take to be sure to win, or cross out the pile if you cannot be sure to win.
edits.fix: Delete "with a bigger pile" (narration; there are three piles); the instruction is otherwise a verbatim repeat of Problem 1 and can be shortened to "It is your turn. Circle the counters you take to be sure to win, or cross out the pile."

edits.quote: Diagram: exactly 5 rows of 4 counters and exactly 8 rows of 5 counters (the exact numbers of 1-or-2 game sequences, 5 and 8).
edits.fix: Print more rows than needed (e.g. 7 and 10) so the page does not reveal how many games exist; deciding when all ways have been found is the problem.

edits.quote: Circle the counters taken on each turn.
edits.fix: Add "Take counters from the left" so the same game circled in different positions is not counted twice and the order of turns can be read from each row.

edits.quote: Diagram: in each pair box, "1st" is printed under the left pile and "2nd" under the right pile.
edits.fix: Center one "1st   2nd" choice below each pair box, away from the individual piles, so children do not read the labels as naming the first and second pile.

k-1.summary: A strong, correct K-1 sequence: concrete piles 1-12 with counters drawn, traps to 20, Ben's fixed opening move, the {1,2,3} rule, two piles with the mirror strategy (including the surprising 1-and-4 pair), and the last-counter-loses variant, with plenty of work for forty minutes. Edits are small: the 1st/2nd labels in Problem 8 sit under individual piles, Problem 6's row counts give away the answer, and Problem 3 repeats Problem 1's wording.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id after a slash, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / G23-1" (template change).

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta wording: "Two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Whoever takes the last counter wins." Each problem already states its allowed moves.

edits.quote: Use the rule from Problem 3: take 1, 3, or 4 counters on each turn. For each starting pile from 1 to 20, decide whether you would rather go first or second.
edits.fix: Keep one statement of the rule and drop the redundant "decide whether you would rather go first or second"; the shading instruction already asks for it.

edits.quote: Diagram: in each pair box, "First" is printed under the left pile and "Second" under the right pile.
edits.fix: Center one "First   Second" choice below each pair box so it is not read as labeling the two piles.

edits.quote: Find a rule for how many counters a player may take on a turn, so that you would rather go second exactly when the starting pile is 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and so on.
edits.fix: Children will try rules without 1 (e.g. take 2 or 3) and reach a pile where nobody can move; add to the shared rules "A player who cannot move loses."

grades-2-3.summary: Mathematically excellent and correct throughout: {1,2} classification, testing Lee's and Mo's claims, the full reply tree for Jo and Kai under {1,3,4}, the period-7 pattern pushed to 100, the parity game {1,3,5}, two piles, and the inverse problem of designing a rule for multiples of 5. Needs only light wording trims, a fix to the First/Second label placement in Problem 7, and a convention for positions with no legal move.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id after a slash, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / G45-1" (template change).

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta wording: "Two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Unless a problem says otherwise, whoever takes the last counter wins."

edits.quote: Dana's plan is to always take as many counters as the rule allows.
edits.fix: Say what the plan does when the pile is smaller than the largest move: "always take the largest allowed number that fits in the pile" (for example, 3 from a pile of 3 in {1, 3, 4}).

edits.quote: Find every game whose allowed moves come from the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 and whose losing piles are exactly the multiples of 4.
edits.fix: Candidate sets without 1 leave a pile where no move is possible; add to the shared rules "A player who cannot move loses." (Answer for the adults: {1,2,3}, {1,2,3,5}, {1,2,3,6}, {1,2,3,5,6}.)

grades-4-5.summary: The strongest band: it classifies {1,3,4} to 24, pushes the period to 2026, compares four rules (including {1,2,4} matching {1,2}), refutes the greedy plan in three games, asks for a periodicity proof and a complete classification of rules giving multiples of 4, and moves to misere play and two-pile grids that bring out non-mirror losing pairs like (1,3), (2,7), (4,6). All answers check; only small wording and convention fixes are needed.

overall.strongest: The grades 4-5 pages build from classifying {1,3,4} through periodicity proof, greedy failure, the inverse problem, misere play, and two-pile grids, with every problem correct and open-ended.
overall.weakest: The K-1 pages need the most fixing, because the 1st/2nd labels in Problem 8 sit under individual piles and Problem 6's preprinted rows give away how many games there are.
